This option is the default selection for BLAST searches.

Swiss-Prot's section of UniProtKB includes manually reviewed protein sequences with high-quality annotations. Swiss-Prot gives the most reliable and well-annotated entries, this is useful if you’re looking for functional information, conserved domains, or known characterized protein families.

Reference proteomes are high-quality, representative sets of protein sequences selected to represent the proteomes of species across the tree of life. These reference proteomes are designed to serve as benchmarks for comparative genomics, evolutionary studies, and functional annotation.

Swiss-Prot data undergoes expert manual curation, so it contains high-quality data but is smaller in scope compared to unreviewed data. Reference proteomes are included in the search to provide wider coverage to supplement Swiss-Prot entries.

the whole of UniProtKB includes both Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL sections, TrEMBL contains computationally analyzed protein sequences that have not been manually reviewed. It is much larger than Swiss-Prot and encompasses more species, however these protein entries are not manually annotated.
This option includes entries in UniProtKB that have a PDB 3D structure
This option includes entries in UniProtKB that have an AlphaFold 3D structure prediction

Reference proteomes are high-quality, representative sets of protein sequences selected to represent the proteomes of species across the tree of life. These reference proteomes are designed to serve as benchmarks for comparative genomics, evolutionary studies, and functional annotation.

Swiss-Prot includes manually reviewed protein sequences with high-quality annotations. Swiss-Prot gives the most reliable and well-annotated entries, this is useful if you’re looking for functional information, conserved domains, or known characterized protein families.
UniRef100 contains all UniProt Knowledgebase records plus selected UniParc records. In UniRef100, all identical sequences and subfragments with 11 or more residues are placed into a single record.

UniRef90 is generated by clustered UniRef100 sequences with 11 or more residues, such that each cluster is composed of sequences that have at least 90% sequence identity to and 90% overlap with the seed sequence.
UniRef50 is built by clustering UniRef90 seed sequences that have at least 50% sequence identity to and 80% overlap with the longest sequence in the cluster.

UniParc (UniProt Archive) is a comprehensive non-redundant protein sequence archive that includes sequences from multiple sources, like GenBank, PDB, and EMBL, updated frequently to capture all known protein sequences.

Select the type based on your input sequence. The type of program will also depend on the type of your input sequence.

Protein (default): Input sequence is an amino acid sequence (protein).
Possible use cases:
Finding homologous proteins in different organisms.
Identifying conserved domains or sites in proteins.
BLAST program: blastp

DNA/RNA: Input sequence is a DNA or RNA sequence (nucleotide)
Possible use cases:
Identifying protein-coding regions in a nucleotide sequence.
Identifying newly sequenced DNA or RNA (e.g., genome or transcriptome data).
Detecting distant homologs where sequence similarity is better detected at the protein level.
BLAST program: blastx

blastp (default): Compares a protein sequence (query) to a protein sequence database.

blastx: Compares a translated nucleotide sequence (query) to a protein sequence database.
Translates the nucleotide sequence into all six possible reading frames (three forward and three reverse).
Compares the resulting protein sequences to the target protein database.

The expectation value (E) threshold is a statistical measure of the number of expected matches in a random database. The lower the e-value, the more likely the match is to be significant. E-values between 0.1 and 10 are generally dubious, and over 10 are unlikely to have biological significance. In all cases, those matches need to be verified manually. You may need to increase the E threshold if you have a very short query sequence, to detect very weak similarities, or similarities in a short region, or if your sequence has a low complexity region.

Min: 0.00001
Max: 1000
Default: 10

The matrix assigns a probability score for each position in an alignment. The BLOSUM matrix assigns a probability score for each position in an alignment that is based on the frequency with which that substitution is known to occur among consensus blocks within related proteins. BLOSUM62 is among the best of the available matrices for detecting weak protein similarities. The PAM set of matrices is also available.

Auto - BLOSUM62 (default)
BLOSUM45
BLOSUM62
BLOSUM80
PAM70
PAM30

Low-complexity regions (e.g. stretches of cysteine in Q03751, or hydrophobic regions in membrane proteins) tend to produce spurious, insignificant matches with sequences in the database which have the same kind of low-complexity regions, but are unrelated biologically. If "Filter low complexity regions" is selected, the query sequence will be run through the program SEG, and all amino acids in low-complexity regions will be replaced by X's.

None (default)
Filter low complexity regions

If ‘yes’ is selected then this will allow gaps to be introduced in the sequences when the comparison is done.

Yes (default)
No

Limits the number of matches returned in the results. Lower the value if you only need top hits, and increase the number if you want a comprehensive list of matches.
